text: Nothing about creating a subnet makes it public or private — AWS has no such flag, no --type public you set at creation. A subnet becomes public purely because its route table sends internet-bound traffic, 0.0.0.0/0, to an Internet Gateway. A private subnet is simply one whose route table has no such route at all. The entire label lives in the routing, not in any property of the subnet itself.

An Internet Gateway, or IGW, is a horizontally scaled, redundant, highly available VPC component that AWS manages for you — there's no instance size to pick and no capacity to plan. It does two things: it's the target a route table points internet traffic at, and it performs the network address translation between an instance's private IP and its public IP. A VPC gets at most one IGW, and it has to be explicitly attached before it does anything at all.

Pointing a subnet's route table at the IGW with a 0.0.0.0/0 route is what makes that subnet public by definition. But the route is only half the story: an instance inside it also needs a public IP address, either auto-assigned at launch or attached afterward as an Elastic IP. Without one, the instance can still initiate outbound connections through the IGW, but nothing on the internet has an address to reach it at directly.

A private subnet has no route to an IGW at all, so nothing inside it is directly reachable from the internet, and typically nothing inside it even has a public IP assigned. That's exactly where a real design puts an application tier or a database tier — instances other parts of the VPC genuinely need to talk to, but that the public internet should never be able to reach directly.

Public means a route to the IGW plus a public IP on the instance; private means neither one is present. Next, Lesson 15 covers how a private-subnet instance still gets outbound internet access — for OS patching, for example — without ever becoming reachable from the outside world.
